title: How Much Time Does It Take to Make a Great Decision
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece lays out a rough framework for how much time different categories of decisions deserve, arguing both too little and too much deliberation produce worse outcomes. Low-stakes decisions warrant seconds to minutes, moderate-consequence choices a few hours to days, and high-stakes decisions a few days to weeks -- with slower deliberation reserved for irreversible, poorly understood, or emotionally charged choices. The author cites research suggesting extra time past a certain point produces analysis paralysis rather than better decisions, and closes with the principle of gathering necessary evidence and then deciding without further delay.
points: Decision time should scale with stakes: seconds for low-consequence choices, hours to days for moderate ones, days to weeks for high-stakes decisions.
Slowing down is specifically warranted when a decision is irreversible, poorly understood, or driven by emotion.
Research cited in the piece suggests extra time past a certain threshold produces overthinking, not better decisions.
The rule of thumb offered: gather the necessary evidence, then decide without further delay -- quality comes from better information, not more calendar time.
quotes: Spending too little or too much time typically leads to poor decisions. So, understanding the time it takes to reach a quality decision is of the utmost importance.
Slowing down the process is wise when the decision is irreversible, poorly understood, or depends on information that is still changing.
Research suggests that after a point, extra time leads to overthinking and analysis paralysis, but not a superior decision.
Smart leaders take the necessary time they need to gather evidence — and not one minute more.
As a rule, leaders allot too much time to make decisions. Faster isn’t always better, but deciding too slowly adds complexity, sows doubt, and encourages second-guessing.
